opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I've gone back and forth on, and I think the honest answer is that the timing matters a great deal, possibly more than people on either side of the debate tend to acknowledge.

The basic worry about an early moratorium is a kind of "crying wolf" dynamic. If you call for a pause at a point where the systems are clearly not yet dangerous, and the pause goes ahead, people may look back and say, "Well, nothing bad happened. That was all a big fuss over nothing." That spends political capital and credibility that you might really need later, when the systems actually are approaching the dangerous capabilities. You might only get one serious shot at a coordinated slowdown, so you want to use it at the moment it buys the most.

There's also a question of what happens during and after the pause. If a moratorium only binds some actors, say a handful of leading labs in a few countries, then development may shift toward less careful groups or less transparent jurisdictions. And when the pause lifts, there can be an overhang: compute has kept getting cheaper, algorithms have kept improving in the background, and so you get a sudden jump in capabilities rather than a gradual climb. A sharp discontinuity like that is arguably more dangerous than steady progress, because it leaves less time for society, regulators, and safety researchers to adapt to each new level.

But I don't think those considerations settle it, because there are real costs to waiting too. The trouble with saying "we'll pause when it's truly dangerous" is that we may not know when that is. These systems have surprised us repeatedly, and the dangerous capabilities might emerge before we have good measurements for them. Political will also takes years to build. You can't spin up international agreements, verification regimes, and compute monitoring overnight. So even if you think the actual pause should come later, you might want to be building the machinery for it now.

So the way I tend to think about it is to separate two things: the decision to actually stop, and the capacity to stop. I'm fairly sympathetic to the view that a full stop right now could be premature and might backfire in the ways I described. But I'm very much in favour of building the capacity now: the institutions, the evaluations that tell us when we're crossing important thresholds, the agreements about what would trigger a slowdown, and the infrastructure to verify compliance. Something like conditional commitments, where everyone agrees in advance that if a system demonstrates certain dangerous capabilities, development pauses until certain safety conditions are met.

That approach captures much of the benefit while avoiding the crying-wolf problem, because the pause is tied to evidence rather than to a date. And it shifts the debate from "are you for or against a pause?", which tends to polarise people, to "what would we need to see, and what would we need to have in place?", which is a question that people with quite different risk estimates can actually make progress on together.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a possible “crying wolf” effect on credibility, but does not say that having a moratorium in place could normalize moratoria.

r002.rationale: It does not mention discouraging investment based on expectations of unrestricted AI development.

r003.rationale: It says to build the capacity for a pause now because agreements and monitoring take time, but does not explain that a moratorium must be called before its intended start date to account for implementation delays.

r004.rationale: The response does not suggest that experience with moratoria would improve the ability to implement them.

fable-5.1.text:
Toby Ord: I think it's one of the hardest questions in the whole area, and I want to be honest that I don't have a settled answer. But let me lay out how I actually think about it.

The case for a moratorium is fairly straightforward. If we're not confident we can make these systems safe, and the downside is potentially unrecoverable, then slowing down buys time. Time for alignment research, time for governance to catch up, time for society to even understand what's happening. On a naive view, delay is almost pure upside when the risk is existential.

But the word "early" is doing a lot of work in your question, and that's where the backfire worries come in. I'd group them into three.

The first is what you might call the overhang problem. Suppose you pause frontier training runs but the underlying inputs keep improving: chips get cheaper, algorithms get more efficient, data keeps accumulating. Then when the pause ends, or when someone defects from it, you don't get a gentle resumption. You get a jump. All that latent capability gets realised at once, and you've traded a gradual ramp that people could study and adapt to for a discontinuity. I take that argument seriously. I don't think it's decisive, because you could in principle pause compute production too, but politically that's far harder.

The second is about who's constrained. A moratorium that only the most safety-conscious actors honour is close to the worst of both worlds. You've removed the labs that were at least trying to do this carefully and handed the frontier to whoever was least willing to sign. That's not an argument against moratoria as such. It's an argument that they need to be close to universal, which means verification and enforcement, which brings us back to compute governance as the thing that actually makes any of this credible.

The third is more about the social dynamics. If you call for a halt before the public has seen anything that looks dangerous, and the predicted harms don't materialise on schedule, you burn credibility. The next time, when the warning really matters, people have already filed you under the boy who cried wolf. There's a real risk that an early, failed moratorium makes a later, necessary one harder to get.

So where does that leave me? I'd say the crux is not "moratorium or not," it's about the mechanism and the timing. I'm much more optimistic about things like mandatory evaluations with the power to stop a deployment, or thresholds on training compute that trigger review, than I am about a blanket indefinite pause declared now. Those get you most of the benefit of slowing down at the dangerous moments without the overhang and defection problems being quite so acute.

And I'd add one thing that I think people on both sides sometimes miss. The argument "it might backfire" is often used as a reason to do nothing. But doing nothing can also backfire. Racing ahead with no brakes has its own failure modes, and they're not symmetric with the failure modes of pausing. When one side of the ledger includes outcomes you can't recover from, I think the burden of proof should sit with those who want to keep accelerating, not with those asking for the ability to stop.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible effects of a moratorium, but does not say that having one in place could normalize moratoria.

r002.rationale: It does not mention discouraging investment premised on unrestricted AI development.

r003.rationale: It discusses the risks of calling for a halt early, but does not explain that implementation delays require calling for a moratorium before its intended start.

r004.rationale: It mentions verification and enforcement challenges, but does not suggest that experience with moratoria could improve the ability to implement them.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a real possibility that it could backfire, but that isn’t a decisive argument against a moratorium. It’s a reason to think carefully about its timing and design.

Suppose you introduce a pause quite early, when the evidence of danger is still contested, and you can only sustain public support for it for a limited time. You might use up that support before reaching the point where a pause is most needed. If the moratorium then collapses, you could find yourself with less trust, less willingness to coordinate, and a renewed race to develop these systems.

But there’s a danger in the opposite direction too. If you always say, “It’s too early; we should wait for clearer evidence,” you might miss the opportunity to act. The evidence might become compelling only when there’s very little time left.

So I’d want to ask: What would the pause actually achieve? What work would continue during it to make us safer? And what conditions would justify resuming development? A pause that creates time for safety research and durable international agreements seems much more valuable than one where we simply wait and then restart the same race. The important thing is whether it leaves us in a better position to manage the danger.

r001.rationale: The response discusses public support for a moratorium, but does not say having one in place could normalize moratoria.

r002.rationale: It does not mention investment or say a moratorium could discourage investment based on unrestricted AI development.

r003.rationale: It considers the risks of an early pause, but does not explain that implementation delays may require calling for a moratorium before its intended start.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that experience with moratoria could improve the ability to implement them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real possibility of that, but we need to be clear about the mechanism. A moratorium could buy us time to understand the risks and work out how to manage them. But if it were imposed before there was enough agreement about why it was needed, it could also undermine the cooperation we’ll need later.

For example, suppose some countries paused while others carried on, or development moved into settings with less oversight. You might end up with less information about what was happening and less ability to influence it. That would be a serious concern.

But I don’t think saying ‘it might backfire’ settles the question. Continuing development might also put us in a much worse position. You have to compare the risks of the particular pause you could actually achieve with the risks of continuing.

So I’d want to ask: Who would participate? What would be paused? How would compliance be checked? And what would we do with the time? A pause linked to a credible process for improving safety and governance seems much more promising than simply stopping and hoping that something changes.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a moratorium’s effects on cooperation and oversight, but does not say it could normalize moratoria.

r002.rationale: It does not mention investment or suggest that a moratorium would discourage investments based on unrestricted AI development.

r003.rationale: It says a moratorium imposed before sufficient agreement could undermine cooperation, but does not explain that implementation delays require calling for one before the desired start time.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that experience with moratoria would improve the ability to implement them.
